Modern.brandNameRationale: Common Good is the classical political-philosophy term for the shared welfare of a community. Foundation is the heritage NGO category suffix. Stands in the lineage of classical-rooted NGO naming.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern nonprofits are competing for attention and donor relationships in a category that has been polished by professionalized fundraising. Donors are design-literate, slightly cynical about overhead, and reward organizations that show clear program work and direct outcomes.
Modern.competitorLandscape: GiveDirectly (givedirectly.org) holds the modern direct-cash-transfer peer position. Charity: Water (charitywater.org) sits in the design-led-fundraising tier. The Trevor Project (thetrevorproject.org) does the cultural-mission middle. We sit closest to GiveDirectly in posture.
Modern.positioningStatement: A nonprofit that shows the program before the appeal.
Modern.positioningRationale: Most nonprofits lead with the donor's feeling. We lead with the program work. The brand promise is that the donor can see exactly what their gift funds before they give.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 55. Already gives to two or three nonprofits annually. Reads charity-evaluator sites. Values transparency on overhead and program outcomes. Will become a recurring donor if the program work is visible.

dos: Speak to the donor as an adult

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark with a small geometric mark to the left. The mark is two thin parallel arcs suggesting open palms, used as the favicon, the donation receipt seal, and the program-report cover.

colorPalette.meaning: Ink, the work on the page.

customSections.title: Where it lives

Modern.brandNameRationale: Proof is what the modern donor demands. The brand puts the only word that matters in the title.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern NGOs split between glossy mission-led brands and rigorous evidence-driven ones. The opportunity is the evidence side, branded with the polish previously reserved for mission marketing.
Modern.competitorLandscape: GiveDirectly (givedirectly.org) holds the evidence-led tier. Charity Navigator (charitynavigator.org) is the institutional precedent. Effective Altruism Funds (funds.effectivealtruism.org) is the donor-aware reference. We sit closest to GiveDirectly in posture.
Modern.positioningStatement: The NGO that shows the receipt for every dollar.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 50. Engineers, product managers, family-office program officers. Donate in the four- or five-figure range annually. Care about cost-per-outcome. Want to see the spreadsheet.
behaviors: Will move money based on a new RCT

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark with a checkmark. PROOF set in a tight grotesk, with a small checkmark above the O suggesting confirmation. The checkmark alone is the favicon.

typography.primary: Söhne for the wordmark and headlines

typography.rationale: Söhne reads modern. Mono carries the numerical evidence.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Three words. The Whitcombe Trust reads as a small, established private foundation. Definite article + family-feeling surname + Trust. The whole name sounds like an institution that has been giving carefully for several generations.
Luxury.story: The Whitcombe Trust was founded by a single family wanting to direct their giving more carefully than mass-market vehicles allowed. The trust accepts no public donations. The endowment is small relative to the giants. The program work is precise.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end philanthropy has been moving toward larger foundations and bigger announcements. There's a parallel market for small family trusts in the older tradition. Smaller endowments, careful grant-making, long-term relationships with grantees. The donor is paying for the trustees, not the brand.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Pew Charitable Trusts (pewtrusts.org) holds the institutional foundation peer. Rockefeller Brothers Fund (rbf.org) sits at the family-foundation tier. Wellcome Trust (wellcome.org) is the international peer. We sit smaller and quieter than all of them.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A small private trust making considered grants to a limited number of grantees.

targetAudience.primary: Wealthy family principals, trustees, and foundation officers managing significant family philanthropy. They value the trustees' judgment and the long relationship with grantees over the announcement of giving.

Luxury.logoDirection: A classical serif wordmark with elegant ligatures. A small hand-drawn family-crest hallmark, two horizontal lines suggesting a heraldic chief, used on letterhead, the grant documents, and the wax seal of every paper letter.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Fitzhugh is a real surname with a long charitable lineage in American letters. Foundation, not fund, signals permanence and institutional intent.
Luxury.industrySummary: Luxury philanthropy serves the family-office donor. Gifts are seven-figure and up, multi-year, often via donor-advised funds. The donor wants institution-building, not feel-good campaigns.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Open Philanthropy (openphilanthropy.org) sets the rigorous-megagift precedent. The Mellon Foundation (mellon.org) is the institutional benchmark. Arnold Ventures (arnoldventures.org) holds the policy-focused tier. We sit between Mellon and Arnold in posture.
Luxury.positioningStatement: An institutional foundation for donors building things meant to outlast them.

targetAudience.primary: 55 to 80. Family principals, foundation trustees, family-office directors. Gift sizes from $5M to $50M annually. Read The Chronicle of Philanthropy. Care about institutional legacy.

Luxury.logoDirection: A wordmark with a seal. THE FITZHUGH FOUNDATION in a classical serif. A circular monogrammed F seal sits above, used on grant letters and building plaques. Embossed only.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word, single verb. Give is what the customer is doing. The brand sits on the action, not the cause, not the institution. Plain, direct, and almost confrontationally simple in a category that usually over-decorates.
Minimal.industrySummary: Most nonprofit brands have elaborate names, mission statements, and donor stories. There's an opening for one that strips it back to the verb itself.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most nonprofit brands fail this purity test. The closest peers in spirit are some giving-circle traditions and the no-name aesthetic of certain donor-advised-fund operators.
Minimal.positioningStatement: A nonprofit with one program, one financial line, and one verb.

targetAudience.primary: Donors who already give and don't want a relationship with the nonprofit. They want to give, see the receipt, and move on.

dos: Show the program, the cost, the impact
Confirm the gift in one line

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Mend is what NGOs do at their best — repair systems, communities, services. One verb, three letters, no qualifier.

Minimal.competitorLandscape: GiveWell (givewell.org) holds the rigorous-minimal slot. Wikimedia (wikimediafoundation.org) is the institutional minimal precedent. Khan Academy (khanacademy.org) sets the operational restraint bar. We sit closest to GiveWell.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Three words. Bedrock signals foundation, permanence, and seriousness. Impact Group names the category. The whole name reads like a real, established philanthropy-services firm already on the panel at major foundations, family offices, and corporate social impact teams.

Corporate.positioningStatement: A civic trust for municipal infrastructure and policy-aligned philanthropy.

Creative.tagline: An NGO for the small repairs.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Civic is the heritage word for matters of citizenship and community. Project frames the work as ongoing. The definite article gives the proper-noun register.
Creative.manifesto: Most nonprofit brands sound like they wish they were more polished than they are. They moralize. They overuse stock photography. They send guilt by email. We made Do Good because the actual work of helping people is loud, fun, exhausting, and worth telling friends about. The brand is for the people who help and also have fun doing it.
Creative.industrySummary: Nonprofit branding has been earnest, beige, and slightly preachy. There's room for a brand that's loud, warm, sticker-friendly, and still serious about the program work that justifies the existence of any nonprofit.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Charity: Water (charitywater.org) does design-led nonprofit well. Pencils of Promise (pencilsofpromise.org) holds the millennial-fundraising peer. The Bail Project (bailproject.org) does the loud-mission middle. We sit warmer and louder than any of them.
Creative.positioningStatement: A nonprofit brand that treats the program work as fun.
